This was scandalous heresy in his day, yet it is also a deep reverence: God is not outside nature; God is this whole, governed by its own necessary laws.

From this follows his determinism: everything happens by necessary cause, and nothing 'could have been otherwise.' That sounds cold, yet Spinoza draws freedom from it — freedom is not doing as you please but 'understanding necessity.' A thrown stone, if conscious, would think it 'wants' to fly; people likewise mistake impulses driven by causes for free will. True freedom is to see clearly the causes that move you, and so pass from passive to active.

His most practical legacy is a geometry of the emotions. In the Ethics he dissects joy, sadness, hope, fear and envy as if proving theorems. The key insight: emotions come in two kinds, passive and active. A passive affect arises from inadequate understanding and enslaves us; once we grasp its cause clearly, it no longer controls us in the same way — an emotion of suffering, he says, ceases to be suffering as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it. Spinoza's salvation, then, is not to repress feeling but to illuminate it with understanding.

He also offers 'conatus' (striving): each being strives to persist in its own existence, the root of all desire and value — we judge a thing good not because it is good in itself but because we desire it. He arrives at last at an 'intellectual love of God (Nature)': when we understand the necessity of all things 'under the aspect of eternity,' narrow fear and resentment loosen, and the mind gains a calm freedom and joy.

assessments.text: 要做一个哲学家，必先成为一个斯宾诺莎主义者——他以此盛赞斯宾诺莎是近代哲学绕不开的起点。
在《西方哲学史》中称他为『伟大哲学家中人格最高尚、最可爱的一位；论智力，有人胜过他，但在伦理上，他至高无上』。
当被问是否信神，他答：『我信仰斯宾诺莎的神——那个在万物有序和谐中显现自身的神。』

assessments_en.text: To be a philosopher one must first be a Spinozist — his way of crowning Spinoza the unavoidable starting point of modern philosophy.
In A History of Western Philosophy he calls him 'the noblest and most lovable of the great philosophers; intellectually some others have surpassed him, but ethically he is supreme.'
Asked whether he believed in God, he replied: 'I believe in Spinoza's God, who reveals himself in the orderly harmony of what exists.'

quotes: 我努力不嘲笑、不哀叹、不诅咒人的行为，而只是去理解它们。
自由的人最少想到死；他的智慧不是对死亡的沉思，而是对生命的沉思。
一种受苦的情感，一旦我们对它形成清晰而明确的观念，就不再是受苦。
凡事愈被理解，就愈在我们的掌握之中，心灵也愈少为它所苦。
quotes_en: I have striven not to laugh at human actions, not to weep at them, nor to hate them, but to understand them.
A free man thinks of nothing less than of death; and his wisdom is a meditation not on death but on life.
An emotion which is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
The more a thing is understood, the more it is within our power, and the less the mind suffers from it.
works_en: Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect (unfinished)
spinoza.lineage: 上承笛卡尔的理性主义与中世纪犹太哲学（迈蒙尼德），旁采斯多葛；下启德国唯心论（黑格尔、谢林），并在 19–20 世纪经由尼采、爱因斯坦、德勒兹不断复活。被列为近代理性主义三巨头（笛卡尔、斯宾诺莎、莱布尼茨）之一，也是《圣经》历史批判与世俗民主思想的先驱。
spinoza.lineage_en: He builds on Descartes's rationalism and medieval Jewish philosophy (Maimonides), drawing also on the Stoics; he opens onto German Idealism (Hegel, Schelling) and is revived again and again across the 19th–20th centuries through Nietzsche, Einstein and Deleuze. He is counted one of the three great rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz) and a forerunner of historical biblical criticism and secular democratic thought.
spinoza.trivia: 他靠磨制光学镜片维生，这门手艺的玻璃粉尘很可能加重了他的肺病；他生前几乎不以真名发表著作，《伦理学》直到死后才面世并迅速被禁；他谢绝了海德堡大学的哲学教授席位，理由是怕公职妨碍思想自由。
spinoza.trivia_en: He earned his living grinding optical lenses, whose glass dust likely worsened his lung disease; he published almost nothing under his own name in his lifetime, and the Ethics appeared only after his death and was quickly banned; he declined a professorship of philosophy at Heidelberg, fearing public office would constrain his freedom of thought.

adamgrant.bio: 亚当·格兰特（1981– ），美国组织心理学家，宾夕法尼亚大学沃顿商学院教授，史上最年轻获终身教职者之一，并连续多年被评为全院最受欢迎的教师。他以严谨实证研究职场动机、慷慨、创造力与韧性著称，著有多部全球畅销书，主持 TED 演讲与热门播客，是当代最具公众影响力的组织心理学家之一。
adamgrant.bio_en: Adam Grant (born 1981) is an American organizational psychologist and a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, one of the youngest people ever tenured there and for years rated its most popular teacher. Known for rigorous empirical work on workplace motivation, generosity, creativity and resilience, he has written several global bestsellers and hosts a TED talk and popular podcasts, making him one of the most publicly influential organizational psychologists of his time.
adamgrant.ideas:
格兰特最广为人知的贡献，是把职场里的人分成三种互动风格：给予者（总想着自己能为别人做什么）、索取者（总想着别人能为自己做什么）、互利者（讲求等价交换、你来我往）。他的反直觉发现是：成功阶梯的最底层和最顶层，都是给予者。差别在于——失败的给予者没有边界，无止境地付出、被索取者白嫖，最终精疲力竭；而最成功的是他称为『otherish』(利他却不自毁)的给予者：既慷慨，又有清醒的自我利益意识，懂得设界、战略性地给。给予者之所以能笑到最后，是因为声誉与善意会随时间复利，而且他们把整块蛋糕做大，而非零和地抢。

由此他重估了一批被低估的特质：比如『难相处的给予者』——嘴上直、爱挑刺，心里却真为你好的人，往往是组织最宝贵却最被嫌弃的资产；又如他对互惠的强调——慷慨不是道德姿态，而是一种长期最优的策略。

在《原创者》(Originals) 里，他研究推动变革的人：原创不等于天生无所畏惧，他们一样会怕、会拖延，只是更善于把熟悉的东西看陌生(vuja de)、广撒点子、并相信『默认值是可以改的』。在《重新思考》(Think Again) 里，他主张最重要的能力之一是质疑自己：别像传教士捍卫信仰、像检察官攻击异见、像政客迎合听众，而要像科学家一样把观点当成待检验的假设，培养『自信的谦逊』，甚至享受发现自己错了的乐趣。在《被低估的潜能》(Hidden Potential) 里，他论证潜能不由起点决定，而靠可后天养成的『性格技能』与一层层搭起的脚手架——过程远比天赋重要。贯穿他全部工作的，是用扎实数据去推翻职场常识：慷慨、谦逊、肯质疑自己的人，反而走得更远。
adamgrant.ideas_en:
Grant is best known for sorting people by three styles of workplace interaction: givers (focused on what they can do for others), takers (on what others can do for them), and matchers (who trade in even exchange). His counterintuitive finding: both the bottom and the very top of the success ladder are givers. The difference is that failed givers have no boundaries — they give endlessly, get freeloaded by takers, and burn out; while the most successful are what he calls 'otherish' givers: generous yet clear-eyed about their own interests, setting boundaries and giving strategically. Givers win in the end because reputation and goodwill compound over time, and because they enlarge the whole pie rather than fight over it zero-sum.

From this he revalues a set of underrated traits: the 'disagreeable giver,' blunt and critical yet genuinely on your side, is often an organization's most valuable and least liked asset; and his stress on reciprocity — generosity not as a moral pose but as the long-run optimal strategy.

In Originals he studies those who drive change: originality is not innate fearlessness — they too feel afraid and procrastinate; they are simply better at seeing the familiar afresh (vuja de), generating many ideas, and believing 'the default can be changed.' In Think Again he argues that one of the most important skills is questioning yourself: don't defend beliefs like a preacher, attack dissent like a prosecutor, or pander like a politician — think like a scientist, treating your views as hypotheses to test, cultivating 'confident humility,' even enjoying the discovery that you were wrong. In Hidden Potential he holds that potential is not fixed by your starting point but built through learnable 'character skills' and scaffolding — process matters far more than raw talent. Running through all his work is the use of hard data to overturn workplace common sense: the generous, the humble, and those willing to doubt themselves tend to go further.

assessments.text: 史上最年轻获终身教职者之一，并连续多年位居全院学生评分最高的教授。
多次入选全球最具影响力管理思想家榜单，以及商业媒体的『40 岁以下 40 人』。
被广泛视为把组织心理学研究带给大众的代表人物，其 TED 演讲累计数千万次观看。

assessments_en.text: One of the youngest people ever tenured there, and for years its highest-rated professor by student reviews.
Repeatedly named among the world's most influential management thinkers, and on business media's '40 under 40.'
Widely seen as the figure who brought organizational-psychology research to a mass audience, with TED talks viewed tens of millions of times.

quotes: 成功最有意义的方式，是帮助别人成功。
像科学家那样思考，而不是像传教士、检察官或政客：把你的观点当成有待检验的假设。（大意）
傲慢是错误的根源，自信的谦逊才是解药——知道自己可能错，正是智识成熟的标志。（大意）
别只在让你点头的信息里打转，去找那些会让你重新思考的人。（大意）
quotes_en: The most meaningful way to succeed is to help others succeed.
Think like a scientist, not a preacher, prosecutor, or politician: treat your views as hypotheses to be tested. (paraphrased)
Arrogance is the root of error; confident humility is the cure — knowing you might be wrong is the mark of intellectual maturity. (paraphrased)
Don't just circle the information that makes you nod; seek out the people who make you rethink. (paraphrased)
works: 《Give and Take（沃顿商学院最受欢迎的成功课）》（2013）
《Option B》（与谢丽尔·桑德伯格合著，2017）
works_en: TED talks and the podcasts WorkLife and Re:Thinking
adamgrant.lineage: 上承社会交换理论与互惠研究（如西奥迪尼的影响力原则），远可追到亚当·斯密对『同情』的洞察；与丹尼尔·平克、苏珊·凯恩、布琳·布朗等当代职场与心理普及作者同代。他的特色是把严谨的学术实证，翻译成普通人用得上的职场智慧。
adamgrant.lineage_en: He builds on social-exchange theory and research on reciprocity (such as Cialdini's principles of influence), reaching back to Adam Smith's insight into sympathy; he is a contemporary of popular work-and-psychology authors like Daniel Pink, Susan Cain and Brené Brown. His signature is translating rigorous empirical research into workplace wisdom ordinary people can use.
adamgrant.trivia: 他年轻时是全美排名的跳板跳水运动员，这段刻意练习的经历塑造了他对『潜能由过程而非天赋决定』的兴趣；他是沃顿最年轻的终身教授之一；他还以一个习惯闻名——公开邀请别人反驳自己，并把『被证明错了』当成乐事。
adamgrant.trivia_en: As a young man he was a nationally ranked springboard diver, and that experience of deliberate practice shaped his interest in potential as a product of process rather than talent; he is one of Wharton's youngest tenured professors; and he is known for a habit of publicly inviting people to prove him wrong and treating 'being wrong' as a delight.
